books.section: Topic 4.3 Politics and Regional Interests, C. A Temporary Truce on the Slavery Question in the Pre-Civil War Period

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the House of Representatives’ gag rule, first adopted in 1836: Any petition or resolution about slavery would be laid on the table without being read, printed, or debated. The rule stayed in force until 1844. Former president John Quincy Adams, then a member of the House from Massachusetts, fought the rule in every session.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the House gag resolutions (Pinckney resolutions), 1836-1844, as described in Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.3 C, and Princeton Review 25e, Chapter 8, 'The Abolition Movement.'

source: original; stimulus paraphrases the House gag rule, 1836-1844, from the grounding books
stem: The gag rule’s long-term effect best shows that

options.text: Congress settled the slavery question in 1836
options.misconception: The slavery question grew after 1836; the rule was repealed in 1844 and the fight went on.
Petitions kept arriving; Adams kept presenting them, and the flood continued.

options.text: silencing debate can spread it, since the rule drew Northerners to abolition
the South gained permanent control of the House of Representatives for decades
options.misconception: The House was based on population, and the North kept growing; the South never held it permanently.

rationales.A: Congress settled nothing in 1836. The rule was repealed in 1844, and the slavery debate only grew louder afterward.
rationales.B: Petitions did not stop. Abolitionists kept sending them, Adams kept forcing them onto the record, and the pile grew every year.
rationales.C: The gag outraged many Northerners who had not cared about abolition, and it convinced them to join the movement. Silencing the debate advertised it.
rationales.D: House seats follow population, and the North’s population kept growing. The South could not hold the House permanently by any rule.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what the rule was meant to do. End the slavery debate in the House.
2. Ask what happened instead. The rule lasted until 1844, and abolition grew through those years.
3. Ask why. Northerners saw a ban on debate as an attack on their right to petition, and many joined the cause.
4. Put it together. The gag did the opposite of its job and spread the debate.
Background: the gag rule, in force from 1836 to 1844, drew outraged Northerners to the abolition movement.
Remember: when a ban backfires, ask who the ban offended beyond its target.
